course.starting_assumption: No programming experience is required. Module 0 starts with your first Python program, then adds data structures, functions, files, Git, and HTTP. Experienced learners can take the placement check, but module projects are still required.
course.time_estimate_note: Lesson estimates include reading and assigned task time where stated. Untimed tasks use a 30-minute planning estimate; module projects take additional time. Treat these as planning ranges, not deadlines.
course.content_maintenance_policy: Version-sensitive implementation lessons are tagged with primary documentation. Review each against its linked source every 90 days; show the verified date and source, and keep unreviewed examples visibly marked in the release queue.

beginner.title: Starting from scratch
beginner.description: Follow the numbered sequence from Module 0. Lessons 0.06 to 0.11 are a hands-on coding ramp: run Python, use lists and dictionaries, write functions, read files, use Git, and call HTTP APIs. Complete every guided practice exercise before opening the worked solution.

experienced.title: Placement check and skip path
experienced.description: Take the ten-question placement check. A score of 8 or more marks the Module 0 and early Module 1 foundation lessons as placed out. The placement never skips module projects, evidence, or the later lessons; those remain the proof that you can build and operate a system.

placement.title: Experienced learner placement check
placement.description: Answer ten questions about the Module 0 and early Module 1 foundations. A score of 8 or more marks those lessons as placed out. Module projects and later lessons are still required.

questions.prompt: Which Python value is a dictionary?
Which exception is raised when a dictionary key is missing?
What is the main purpose of a virtual environment?
Which Git command records staged changes?
Which file should normally be excluded from Git?
Which status codes are usually safe to retry?
What does a function return statement do?
options: Hands a value back to the caller

questions.prompt: Why add type hints to a function?
options: They document intended types and help tools

00.assumed_prerequisites: None. Start here if you are new to AI engineering.
00.readiness_check: Explain the user problem, model boundary, data flow, and one reason a deterministic system may be safer than an LLM.
project_deliverables: One-page AI system glossary
Architecture sketch showing model, data, tools, application, and operations boundaries

project_rubric.criterion: Concepts are accurate and distinguish model behavior from application guarantees.
Architecture sketch labels request, data, and trust boundaries.
A beginner can explain the sketch without relying on unexplained jargon.

01.assumed_prerequisites: Complete Module 0, or pass the placement check. You should be able to run a Python file, use lists and dictionaries, write a small function, read a traceback, and make a Git commit. Module projects are still required after placement.
01.readiness_check: Build a small typed Python package with validation, bounded HTTP calls, and automated tests.
project_deliverables: Installable Python API client
Typed response models and bounded timeout/retry behavior
Automated tests using a fake transport

project_rubric.criterion: Client validates inputs and provider responses.
Timeout and retry behavior is bounded and does not retry permanent failures.
Automated tests cover success, malformed output, and provider failure.

02.assumed_prerequisites: Python functions, collections, exceptions, HTTP and JSON; able to run a small Python test.
02.readiness_check: Run an API and database locally; demonstrate validation, authorization, migrations, and one failure path.
project_deliverables: FastAPI service with PostgreSQL persistence
Migration and authorization checks
Redis or queue use justified by a measured requirement
API tests for success and failure cases

project_rubric.criterion: API contracts and authorization are enforced at the server boundary.
Persistence and migrations work from a clean database.
Automated tests cover validation, isolation, and a failure path.

03.assumed_prerequisites: Python basics, HTTP requests, JSON, and basic probability (fractions and averages).
03.readiness_check: Explain tokens and sampling, estimate a prompt budget, and compare model outputs on a fixed set of cases.
project_deliverables: Model capability and cost comparison on a frozen task set
Token budget calculator
Short report separating model errors from system errors

project_rubric.criterion: Model comparison uses a fixed representative dataset and records variability.
Token, latency, and cost estimates state their assumptions.
Recommendations distinguish model limitations from deterministic system responsibilities.

04.assumed_prerequisites: Module 3 concepts and the ability to call a model API with a typed request and response.
04.readiness_check: Run a model-backed endpoint that validates structured output, handles provider errors, and records token/cost data.
project_deliverables: Model-backed document endpoint
Validated structured response contract
Timeout, provider error, trace, and cost behavior demonstrated

project_rubric.criterion: Structured outputs are validated before business logic uses them.
Provider failures respect an overall deadline and produce a defined response.
Logs or traces identify request, model, latency, tokens, and outcome without secrets.

05.assumed_prerequisites: LLM API calls, embeddings as vectors, and basic database concepts.
05.readiness_check: Retrieve relevant evidence from a small corpus, cite source locations, and report retrieval quality on labeled queries.
project_deliverables: Ingestion and retrieval pipeline over a small corpus
Citations with source locations and permission filtering
Labeled retrieval evaluation with at least one failure analysis

project_rubric.criterion: Ingestion is repeatable and preserves source provenance and access rules.
Retrieval outputs citations that resolve to real source locations.
Evaluation reports retrieval quality and includes a failure analysis.

06.assumed_prerequisites: Python functions, API calls, tool schemas, and authorization basics.
06.readiness_check: Run an agent with allowlisted tools, bounded steps and spend, validated arguments, and a stop condition.
project_deliverables: Tool-using agent with bounded steps and spend
Allowlist and authorization checks
Tests for invalid tool arguments and stop conditions

project_rubric.criterion: Tools use schemas, allowlists, authorization, and bounded execution.
Agent runs stop on success, denial, error, or budget exhaustion.
Tests prove invalid arguments and unauthorized actions cannot execute.

07.assumed_prerequisites: A working single-agent loop, tool calls, and persisted application state.
07.readiness_check: Resume a multi-step workflow from saved state and show a human approval or recovery path.
project_deliverables: Resumable workflow with explicit state and transitions
Checkpoint and recovery demonstration
Human approval path and event trace

project_rubric.criterion: Workflow state and transitions are explicit and validated.
A failed or interrupted run can resume without duplicating side effects.
Human approval, recovery, and trace evidence are demonstrated.

08.assumed_prerequisites: JSON-RPC basics, HTTP or stdio, tool schemas, and server-side authorization.
08.readiness_check: Connect a client to a server, discover or negotiate its capabilities, and enforce least-privilege tool access.
project_deliverables: MCP client and server interoperability demo
Version/capability discovery or negotiation documented
Tool permissions, authentication, and denied-call case demonstrated

project_rubric.criterion: Client/server behavior follows a named MCP protocol version and documents compatibility.
Authentication and tool authorization are enforced outside model instructions.
A denied or malformed tool call is tested and recorded.

09.assumed_prerequisites: A small API service, model integration, retrieval or tool use, and basic automated tests.
09.readiness_check: Show a repeatable evaluation, trace, security check, load result, and cost/latency budget for an AI feature.
project_deliverables: Production readiness pack for the AI service
Evaluation and red-team cases
Trace, load result, cost budget, and rollback procedure

project_rubric.criterion: Evaluation cases cover quality, safety, and regression risks.
Load, observability, and per-request cost evidence are reproducible.
Release and rollback criteria are explicit and tied to measured thresholds.

10.assumed_prerequisites: A tested Python service, Git basics, environment variables, and HTTP/database fundamentals.
10.readiness_check: Build and run a reproducible container, deploy it through a documented pipeline, and explain rollback and secret handling.
project_deliverables: Container build pinned to a reviewed base image
CI build and deployment instructions
Health check, secrets configuration, and rollback notes

project_rubric.criterion: Image uses reviewed, reproducible inputs and runs as a non-root service where feasible.
CI verifies image build and health; deployment configuration keeps secrets external.
Rollback and persistent-data behavior are documented.

11.assumed_prerequisites: Working knowledge of backend, LLM, retrieval, agent, security, and deployment trade-offs.
11.readiness_check: Present a system design with measured requirements, data and state flows, trust boundaries, and failure budgets.
project_deliverables: Context, data, request, and state diagrams
Requirements-to-tests traceability matrix
Decision records with latency, cost, security, and failure budgets

project_rubric.criterion: Requirements have observable thresholds and linked tests or evaluations.
Diagrams show request, data, state, ownership, and trust boundaries.
Trade-offs include quantified latency, cost, security, and degraded behavior.

12.assumed_prerequisites: Artifacts from prior modules or equivalent evidence: tested service, evaluation set, deployment plan, and architecture decisions.
12.readiness_check: Demonstrate a deployed AI system against acceptance checks, evaluation results, operational budgets, and a documented rollback.
project_deliverables: Running production-style AI platform
Automated acceptance and quality evaluation suite
Deployment, operations, security, cost, and rollback evidence

project_rubric.criterion: Acceptance checks and evaluations pass on the submitted revision.
Deployment is reproducible and operational behavior is observable.
Security, cost, failure, data handling, and rollback evidence is included.

8.01.subtitle: Understand MCP as a versioned contract, including current stateless requests and legacy handshake compatibility.
outcomes: Explain how an MCP host, client, and server divide discovery, consent, and execution without custom glue code.
Identify tools, resources, and prompts, and distinguish current stateless discovery from the legacy initialize handshake.
Decide when MCP is preferable to a direct API call, library, or fixed workflow.
tasks: Draw a host-client-server diagram for one assistant you use, naming transports, trust boundaries, and where user consent is enforced.
Write a one-page decision record choosing MCP or a direct API for two integrations, with explicit interoperability and operations criteria.

Use an inspector or fixture to capture a modern server/discover or tools/call request, then compare it with an initialize exchange from a handshake-era peer. CAPSTONE CONNECTION The capstone will document supported protocol versions and enforce user consent and per-server credentials at the host.

code.title: A current stateless MCP request and the legacy handshake shown for compatibility.

steps: List the external systems an assistant needs, marking each as read-only, write, or high-risk.
For each system, write the three most valuable operations and the data they return.
Decide which operations fit tools, which fit resources, and which need a prompt template.
Choose stdio for local, user-scoped servers and Streamable HTTP for shared, authenticated services.
Inspect a modern server/discover or tools/call request, then compare it with initialize and tools/list on a handshake-era peer.
production_notes: The 2026-07-28 protocol is stateless and does not use initialize; older peers still negotiate a handshake. Record the versions your client supports.
A protocol handshake or discovery response is not authorization. Enforce user, tenant, and tool permissions at the host and server.
Give every server its own credentials, network egress rules, and audit stream so one compromise does not span systems.
Monitor discovery or handshake failures, tool error rates, and p95 call latency per server.
checklist: I can name the host, client, server, and transport in an MCP request.
I can distinguish tools, resources, and prompts by their effect.
I know why the host, not the server, owns user consent.
I can explain when a direct API call is simpler than MCP.
I can identify a current stateless request and a legacy initialize exchange.

8.03.subtitle: Understand the handshake-era protocol and the stateless 2026 protocol, then select compatible SDK behavior deliberately.
outcomes: Distinguish handshake-era and 2026 stateless MCP requests.
Select stdio or Streamable HTTP independently from protocol lifecycle.
Build a compatibility test matrix for client, server, SDK, and protocol revisions.
tasks: Build a protocol and SDK compatibility matrix for the peers you support.
Test one current and one handshake-era peer or fixture.

code.title: Route modern stateless requests and legacy handshake-era requests by their protocol version.

8.12.subtitle: Operate versioned MCP servers with capability ownership, safe protocol upgrades, authorization, and observable compatibility.
outcomes: Design a registry entry with protocol and SDK compatibility.
Plan a staged upgrade across handshake-era and stateless peers.
Define observability and security controls at host, gateway, and server boundaries.
tasks: Build a protocol and SDK compatibility matrix for the peers you support.
Test one current and one handshake-era peer or fixture.

code.title: A registry gate that records protocol versions and requires a tested compatibility policy.

tasks: Scaffold a server for one owned dataset with environment configuration, stderr logging, and a startup check.
Expose one tool, one resource template, and one prompt, then write ten tests including a traversal attempt.
Capture server/discover for a stateless peer or initialize for a legacy peer, document the protocol version, and write a 300-word review request naming limits and owner.
Connect an agent to two MCP servers, convert their schemas, and count how many tools the model actually sees.
Add step and time budgets plus duplicate detection, then replay ten questions and record completion and latency.
Test modern discovery and a handshake-era fallback; map three failure classes to retry policy, model-visible message, and trace field.
